solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: A Bovril, if stirred, source of nutritious vitamin

indicators.note: stirring mixes the contents of a pot, so these letters are jumbled into a new order
a source is where something starts, so only the opening letter of the next word is used

blocks.note: the letters taken as written, ready to be mixed
the first letter of this word

explanation.surface: Someone stirring a mug of Bovril, the beef-extract drink, is told it is a source of a nutritious vitamin.
explanation.walkthrough: Bovril is a salty British meat-extract paste made into a hot drink. 'If' looks like a conjunction but is just two more letters of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Riboflavin is the chemical name for vitamin B2, so it is a specific example of a vitamin.

clue.text: Expensive watch missing last part

indicators.note: missing something means lacking it, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: a famous luxury Swiss watch brand

explanation.surface: A pricey wristwatch has lost one of its components.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last part' reads as one phrase, but 'last' belongs to the deletion and 'part' is the definition on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor's role is the part played in a production, so the two are everyday synonyms.

clue.text: Talked spitefully about support section

blocks.note: to back someone is to support them
a bit is a piece or section

explanation.surface: Someone spoke nastily about a part of a support structure, or a group of supporters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like a container or link word, but it belongs to the definition, which needs it to be transitive.
explanation.definitionFit: To backbite is to speak maliciously of someone absent; its past tense matches 'talked spitefully about'.

clue.text: Continental insect – leg protection is essential here

blocks.note: from the European continent, here France
a chirping, jumping insect

explanation.surface: A European bug is introduced, followed by a remark that shin guards are vital somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: French cricket is a children's garden game in which the batter's legs act as the wicket, so the bat must guard them.
explanation.definitionFit: In this informal game the ball must not strike the batter's legs below the knee, so defending the lower limbs is the whole point.

clue.text: Saw leaders in Home Office grabbed by a solid figure

indicators.note: leaders go at the front, so only the opening letters of the following words count
whatever is grabbed is held inside the grabber's grip, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: taken as written
a prism is a three-dimensional geometric solid
the initials of the British government department

explanation.surface: Someone saw the senior figures of the Home Office, the UK interior ministry, held by a stout person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' looks like the past tense of see, but it is the noun meaning an old saying.
explanation.definitionFit: A saw is a traditional proverb or maxim, and an aphorism is a short pithy statement of general truth.

clue.text: Test side batting: 501 latest from Kolkata

indicators.note: the latest of anything is its most recent or final one, so the closing letter is taken

blocks.note: a batter currently batting is said to be in
Roman numerals: D is 500 and I is 1
the final letter of the city's name

explanation.surface: A cricket score update: a Test team batting has reached 501, with the latest news from Kolkata.
explanation.walkthrough: A Test is an international cricket match; 501 looks like a cricket score but is split into Roman numerals.
explanation.definitionFit: The national cricket team of that country plays Test matches, so it is a Test-playing side.

clue.text: Reptile starts to chew really old carrion

indicators.note: starts are beginnings, so the opening letter of each following word is kept

blocks.note: the first letter of each of the four words

explanation.surface: A reptile begins to chomp on rotting, very old carcass meat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starts to chew' reads as beginning to eat, but 'starts' covers all four words that follow.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the short informal name for a crocodile, a large scaly reptile.

clue.text: Government plane, MiG, erratically circles about

indicators.note: to circle something is to surround it, so the run of text encloses the letters wanted
turning about means facing the other way, so the letters are read backwards

blocks.note: a run of letters straddling the three words

explanation.surface: A government aircraft, a Russian fighter, flies in wild loops.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Erratically' looks like an anagram signal, but it only supplies two letters at the end of the hidden run, read from right to left.
explanation.definitionFit: Regimen in its older sense means rule or a system of governing, though today it usually means a regulated plan such as a diet.

clue.text: The King put on a lot of weight in US city

indicators.note: to put something on is to add it, so one piece is attached to the next

blocks.note: the current British monarch, King Charles III
a ton is a large unit of weight

explanation.surface: The monarch gained a great deal of weight while visiting an American city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put on a lot of weight' reads as getting fat; 'put on' simply attaches the weight after the King.
explanation.definitionFit: Charleston is a historic port in South Carolina, and also the capital of West Virginia.

clue.text: Tempt banks about wealth

indicators.note: banks line both sides of a river, so one piece sits on either side of another

blocks.note: to lure is to tempt or entice
c is short for circa, Latin for about

explanation.surface: Someone tempts banks with the promise of riches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banks' looks like financial institutions, fitting 'wealth', but it is a verb here: the first word's letters flank the second's.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucre is money or profit, usually with a disapproving tone, as in 'filthy lucre'.

clue.text: Park warden discussed plant

indicators.note: something discussed is spoken about, so the words are heard rather than read

blocks.note: Hyde Park is in London and a ranger is a park warden

explanation.surface: A park keeper talked about some vegetation.
explanation.walkthrough: Hyde Park is a large royal park in central London; its warden would be a ranger. Said in a non-rhotic British accent, the two run together.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a flowering garden shrub with large rounded heads of blue, pink or white blooms.

clue.text: Clumsy Geordie perhaps collecting papers lying on the floor

indicators.note: to collect something is to gather it in, so one piece takes another inside it

blocks.note: a Geordie is someone from Newcastle, known for a distinctive way of speaking
identity papers, ID for short
lying face down

explanation.surface: A clumsy man from Newcastle picks up newspapers strewn on the floor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' marks an example: a Geordie accent is one kind of accent. 'Papers' suggests newspapers but means identity documents.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who keeps having mishaps through awkwardness is clumsy, so the compound adjective is a close synonym.

clue.text: Silly act with balancer? I’m one getting the hump

indicators.note: silly means foolish or nonsensical, so these letters are jumbled into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A circus balancing performer's routine is mocked as silly, and they say it puts them in a sulk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I’m' looks like part of the speaker's sentence but adds its letters to the mix. In British slang, to get the hump is to get annoyed.
explanation.definitionFit: This two-humped Asian camel literally acquires humps, punning on the British idiom for becoming grumpy.

clue.text: Rigid line FBI applied around law

indicators.note: something applied is put to work in a new way, so these letters are reworked into a fresh order
around means surrounding, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: the letters taken as written, ready to be rearranged
lex is Latin for law

explanation.surface: The FBI took a hard line in enforcing the law.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Line' and 'Rigid' look like they belong together, but 'line' is fodder for the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something stiff that will not bend, or a person unwilling to change their mind.

clue.text: Famous college backed legal action – there’s money in it

indicators.note: going backwards means heading the other way, so the letters run from right to left

blocks.note: Eton is a well-known English public school
a lawsuit is a case

explanation.surface: A posh school supports a lawsuit, because there is cash to be made from it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Backed' seems to mean supported, but it turns the school round. Eton College is the famous boarding school near Windsor.
explanation.definitionFit: A notecase is an old-fashioned British word for a wallet, which holds banknotes.

clue.text: Area Mafia boss is a good-looking lad

blocks.note: A is the standard abbreviation for area
the usual title for the head of a Mafia family
taken as written

explanation.surface: The local crime boss is described as a handsome young man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Is' looks like the link to the definition, but it supplies the final letters, so there is no link word.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth Adonis was a beautiful youth loved by Aphrodite, so his name stands for any handsome young man.

clue.text: We arrest suspect Tube pest

indicators.note: something suspect is dubious or not right, so these letters are out of order

blocks.note: the letters taken as written, ready to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Police announce they are detaining a suspected nuisance on the London Underground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Suspect' looks like a noun for the person arrested, but it is an adjective signalling the mix. The Tube is London's Underground; here a tube is any pipe.
explanation.definitionFit: This brown rodent lives in drains and pipes, so it is a pest found in tubes underground.

clue.text: Dog star?

blocks.note: surface reading: Sirius, the bright star in the constellation Canis Major
setter's reading: a canine that is a celebrity, the collie of film and television fame

explanation.walkthrough: The Dog Star is the astronomical name for Sirius; the question mark tells you to read it as a famous dog instead.
explanation.definitionFit: The rough collie from the 1943 film and long-running TV series is the best-known canine screen celebrity.

clue.text: Ryman’s first to carry main item of office equipment

indicators.note: first means the leading one, so only the opening letter of the word is used
a carrier bears a load on its back, so one piece is set after the other

blocks.note: staple as an adjective means chief or principal
the opening letter of the shop's name

explanation.surface: The stationery chain's top priority is to stock its principal office product.
explanation.walkthrough: Ryman is a British high-street stationery chain, which makes the surface apt. 'Main item' looks like one phrase; 'main' belongs to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A desk device that drives wire fasteners through paper is a standard piece of office kit.

clue.text: Leg breaking ordeal tormented Italian genius

indicators.note: something tormented is twisted in agony, so these letters are wrenched into a new order
breaking into something means getting inside it, so one piece is placed within another

blocks.note: the letters taken as written, ready to be rearranged
in cricket the leg side is also called the on side

explanation.surface: Someone suffered a terrible broken-leg ordeal and a tortured Italian genius endured it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leg breaking' reads as a fracture, but it is a cricket term: the leg side of the field is the on side.
explanation.definitionFit: Leonardo da Vinci, painter, inventor and scientist of the Renaissance, is the archetypal Italian polymath.

clue.text: Engineers can uncouple empty train

indicators.note: an empty container has nothing inside, so only the outer letters remain

blocks.note: the Royal Engineers, a British army corps
a tin is a can
the first and last letters of the word

explanation.surface: Railway engineers are able to detach the carriages of an empty train.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Train' and 'uncouple' paint a railway; 'train' is in fact the line of followers behind a dignitary.
explanation.definitionFit: A retinue is the group of attendants following an important person, which is one sense of a train.

clue.text: 10 points: actor turning to phrase from Treasure Island

indicators.note: turning round faces the other way, so these letters are read from right to left

blocks.note: X is the Roman numeral for ten
marks are points scored in a test
a thesp is short for thespian, an actor
taken as written

explanation.surface: A critic awards ten points to an actor who turns to a line from Stevenson's pirate novel.
explanation.walkthrough: '10' looks like a cross-reference to another clue or a score, but it is a Roman numeral; 'turning' reverses only the little word after it.
explanation.definitionFit: The saying about a cross on a treasure map is popularly associated with the pirate adventure, so it counts as a phrase from the book.

clue.text: Absorbent cloth – keep changing hands

indicators.note: hands are right and left, so one of those letters is swapped for the other

blocks.note: a keep is the main tower of a castle

explanation.surface: A cloth that soaks up water keeps being passed from person to person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Changing hands' usually means changing owner; here the R (right) at the end is replaced by L (left).
explanation.definitionFit: A towel is a piece of thick fabric used for drying, so it is literally an absorbent cloth.

clue.text: Exploit European article in newspaper

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so these pieces go within another

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for European
the indefinite article
the Financial Times, a London business daily

explanation.surface: Someone takes advantage of a story about Europe printed in a paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exploit' looks like a verb, but it is the noun meaning a daring deed.
explanation.definitionFit: An exploit is a bold or remarkable achievement, which is exactly what a feat is.

clue.text: Call tug “Campanile”

blocks.note: to give someone a bell is British slang for phoning them
a tug is a boat that tows, so it is a tower

explanation.surface: Someone radios a harbour tugboat that happens to be named after an Italian bell tower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tug' must be read as a thing that tows; 'tower' here rhymes with 'mower', not 'flower'.
explanation.definitionFit: Campanile is the Italian word, used in English, for a freestanding structure housing church bells.

clue.text: Doorman when undressed is a unit

indicators.note: undressing strips off the outer layer, so the first and last letters are removed

blocks.note: a bouncer guards the door of a club

explanation.surface: A nightclub doorman stripped of his uniform is just a member of a military unit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unit' hints at a soldier, but it is a unit of measurement.
explanation.definitionFit: An ounce is an imperial measure of weight, about 28 grams, so it is a unit.

clue.text: Noble, tragic king left at the back

indicators.note: L is short for left, and putting it at the back moves that letter from the front to the end

blocks.note: King Lear, Shakespeare's tragedy

explanation.surface: A noble, doomed monarch has been abandoned at the rear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like 'abandoned', but it identifies the letter that moves from the front of the king's name to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: An earl is a British peer ranking below a marquess, so a member of the nobility.

clue.text: Farewell greatest hits album?

blocks.note: first meaning: a parting good wish
second meaning: a compilation of an artist's top songs

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the second meaning is playful: a compilation would literally contain every top track.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a common goodbye sign-off, and also a plausible title for a compilation of an artist's top tracks.
